title: Narwhals: Unicorns of the Sea
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the narwhal, the Arctic toothed whale known for its long spiral tusk. They cover the name and the corpse-whale nickname, the historical belief in unicorns and the tusks sold as unicorn horns, its habitat in polynyas and under sea ice, its diet and deep dives, echolocation and intelligence, population and genetic homogeneity, the function of the tusk (sensory organ, possible secondary sex characteristic), hunting by Inuit and poaching, and threats from orcas and melting sea ice. The episode closes with a listener mail about the origin of the two-fingered salute.
topics: Stuff You Should Know narwhal episode

segments.title: Opening and tour announcements
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck announce fall tour dates in Salt Lake City, Phoenix and Melbourne, then introduce the narwhal topic and credit former colleague Katie Lambert's article.

segments.title: Narwhal basics and unicorn horn myths
segments.summary: The narwhal is a small, fast Arctic whale with a tusk often over half its body length; males reach about fifteen feet. Its tusk was traded from Greenland and sold as unicorn horn, used in items for the Habsburg scepter, Ivan the Terrible's staff, and the English pharmacists' coat of arms.

segments.title: Name, corpse whale nickname, and habitat
segments.summary: The Latin name Monodon monoceros is explained, with the hosts noting the animal has two teeth, not one horn. Narwhals are called corpse whales because of their mottled coloring, and the Dutch and Danish name means corpse whale. They navigate polynyas under ice and lack a dorsal fin, having a ridge instead, which helps them escape orcas.

segments.title: Diet, group size, speed and deep diving
segments.summary: Narwhals live in groups of twenty to thirty, sometimes hundreds or thousands while migrating. They eat cod, halibut, herring, salmon, shrimp and squid, and have been tracked diving about a mile deep. Early tracking devices broke under pressure.

segments.title: Echolocation, intelligence and culture
segments.summary: Narwhals are considered very smart, with abilities comparable to dolphins and some abilities only apes show. They echolocate, producing sound through nasal passages and the melon, and may use different frequencies for near and far targets. Brain size is said to be second only to humans relative to body mass. Culture is passed between generations.

segments.title: Lifespan, population and genetic bottleneck
segments.summary: Some studies suggest narwhals may live over a hundred years, with one estimate of 115 years from eye lens study. Over thirty thousand were counted in Baffin Bay. Polynyas are sites of mating but also deadly ice traps. Narwhals are genetically homogeneous, likely due to a past evolutionary bottleneck from die-offs in frozen polynyas.

segments.title: The tusk: structure, function and Darwin's theory
segments.summary: The tusk is a spiral tooth growing through the lip, sensitive on the outside with about ten million tiny holes, unlike human teeth. Possible functions include sensing salinity, temperature, currents and pressure. Darwin's secondary sex characteristic hypothesis is still the most widely held, though few females have tusks. Tusking behavior appears gentle, and the tusk is flexible, bending up to a foot. Two tusks can occasionally occur.

segments.title: Hunting, poaching, Inuit use and climate threats
segments.summary: Inuit are allowed to hunt narwhals in set numbers, sometimes with harpoons and rifles. Poachers have killed narwhals only for tusks. Muktuk, the skin and blubber, is an important vitamin C source for Inuit. Orcas, polar bears and walruses prey on narwhals, and climate change melting sea ice is a major threat; narwhals were called among the marine mammals least likely to survive.

segments.title: Listener mail: two-fingered salute origin
segments.summary: Listener Daniel Halifax from Doncaster, England, writes that the two-fingered salute dates to the Hundred Years War, when French captors cut off English longbowmen's index and middle fingers, so archers taunted the French by raising two fingers.

segments.title: Closing and contact info
